precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (en banc)
precedents.holding: An ADA plaintiff who encountered at least one barrier related to his disability, and is deterred or intends to return, has standing to challenge other unencountered barriers related to that disability, but must plead which barriers he encountered and how they affected him.
precedents.topic: standing and pleading: why findings must name the specific barrier and the disability it affects

verification.note: Reporter citation 631 F.3d 939, date 2011-01-07 and docket 07-16326 confirmed on OpenJurist; holding matches the opinion (standing for related unencountered barriers; Chapman lacked standing because he never pleaded how barriers affected him).

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: A store that repeatedly let merchandise and displays obstruct its aisles violated Title III; recurring obstructions are not the isolated or temporary interruptions excused by 28 C.F.R. 36.211(b).
precedents.topic: movable merchandise counts against route width

verification.note: Carried over from the v1 precedent table, verified by Boris Nezlobin on 2026-09-30.

precedents.holding: Registers and promotional items kept the usable point-of-sale counter under the 36 in length 904.4.1 requires, and display baskets formed an alcove deeper than 15 in and narrower than 60 in (305.7.2); routinely placed items are not temporary obstructions.
precedents.topic: counter length kept clear; displays forming alcoves

verification.note: Carried over from the v1 precedent table, verified by Boris Nezlobin.

precedents.holding: Interior accessible tables that left a wheelchair user facing the wall denied full and equal enjoyment under 42 U.S.C. 12182(b)(1); the court ordered at least one interior accessible table where a wheelchair user can face into the store.

verification.note: Carried over from the v1 precedent table, verified by Boris Nezlobin.

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: Affirmed the point-of-sale counter ruling (recurring, not temporary, barriers) and the interior seating finding, but vacated ADA injunctive relief as moot after the plaintiff's death while Unruh Act damages survived.
precedents.topic: appellate confirmation; Unruh damages survive mootness of ADA relief

verification.note: Read from the Ninth Circuit PDF. Non-precedential under Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3.

precedents.holding: Findings of fact and conclusions of law after a June 2011 bench trial in the class action over access at California Taco Bell restaurants: violations found for each of 12 elements at an exemplar store (parking and signage, doors, queue lines, tables, restrooms), with classwide injunctive relief appropriate.
precedents.topic: fast-food restaurant queue lines, counters and door force

verification.note: Court, docket 4:02-cv-05849, ECF 642 and 2011-10-05 confirmed from Clearinghouse; the 816 F. Supp. 2d 831 cite appears only on Clearinghouse. Holding revised to what Clearinghouse reports: after a June 2011 bench trial the court found violations at all 12 elements of an exemplar store (parking and signage, doors, queues, tables, restrooms) and kept classwide injunctive relief. The opinion text itself was not read.

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: An ADA complaint that only alleged inaccessible service counters, without saying how they denied access (for example too high or too low), failed to state a claim.
precedents.topic: findings must state the measured value and limit, not just 'inaccessible'

verification.note: Citation 985 F.3d 1173, docket 19-56497 and filed 2021-01-25 confirmed on OpenJurist; dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) affirmed because the complaint did not say how the counters denied access.

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: An ADA plaintiff must identify each barrier in the complaint to give fair notice; barriers raised first in a later expert report were properly excluded.
precedents.topic: each finding is a separately identified barrier (report design)

verification.note: Citation 654 F.3d 903, docket 09-56447 and filed 2011-08-17 confirmed on OpenJurist; barriers raised only in an expert report, not the complaint, were not properly before the court (Rule 8).

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: The district court abused its discretion by denying a new trial: the jury's 'No' to whether the restaurant failed to identify and remove architectural barriers had no evidentiary support (the defendant admitted the barriers existed and that no one tried to identify or remove them). Judgment vacated and remanded for new trial. The $4,000 Unruh damages question and readily-achievable removal were never reached.
precedents.topic: readily achievable restroom fixes (grab bars, pipe insulation, partitions, dispensers)

verification.note: Citation 481 F.3d 724, filed 2007-03-23, caption and CV-03-04809-DT confirmed on Justia. Holding corrected: the prior text said the jury found barriers removed and that $4,000 requires no proof of damages; the opinion does neither (it only quotes the Unruh minimum).

precedents.holding: A plaintiff who proves an ADA access violation need not prove intentional discrimination to recover Unruh Act damages under Civil Code 52.
precedents.topic: every ADA rule failure is an Unruh violation in California

verification.note: Citation, date and holding read from the Stanford SCOCAL page.

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: A lay witness present during measurements can testify to observed conditions without an expert, and the 'readily achievable' burden applies only to facilities built before January 26, 1993.
precedents.topic: measured evidence from a scan supports findings; construction era sets the legal standard

verification.note: Citation 724 F.3d 1042 and docket 11-55265 confirmed on OpenJurist, which gives the decision date as 2013-07-18 (corrected from 2013-07-22). Holding confirmed: lay personal observations can create a fact question; readily-achievable proof not required for new construction (42 USC 12183(a)). The case concerns a restaurant, not parking.

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: A serial ADA litigant had standing, a customer parking lot is a Title III facility, and courts may not discount intent to return because the plaintiff files many suits.
precedents.topic: parking lots are covered; tester plaintiffs have standing

verification.note: Caption, docket 21-55183, filing date 2023-01-23 and holding confirmed from the Ninth Circuit PDF, Justia and Willamette summaries. The 57 F.4th 1085 reporter cite could not be confirmed from any source reachable here (CourtListener and Justia reporter pages blocked); remains unverified.

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: A plaintiff with standing based on at least one barrier related to his disability may challenge all barriers at the facility related to that disability, including those found only through his expert's inspection; summary judgment affirmed on aisle width and the employees-only restroom (not a public accommodation); supplemental jurisdiction ruling vacated.
precedents.topic: why the scan checks every element, not just the plaintiff's path

verification.note: Superseding opinion filed 2008-05-02 (panel rehearing granted, withdrawing the 2007-11-09 opinion at 506 F.3d 1191); 524 F.3d 1034 and docket 05-56439 confirmed on OpenJurist and Justia.

precedents.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
precedents.holding: Lay testimony estimating a checkout counter above 36 in can support a violation without an expert; a dressing room bench longer than required did not violate the ADA where a parallel transfer was possible.
precedents.topic: counter height evidence; bench length is a minimum

precedents.case_name: ADA Update: A Primer for Small Business
precedents.citation: U.S. Dep't of Justice, Civil Rights Division (March 2011)
precedents.holding: Barrier removal is a continuing obligation; elements complying with the 1991 Standards keep safe harbor element by element; where an accessible counter is not readily achievable, provide a folding shelf or nearby accessible counter, and some accessible tables must be dispersed in dining areas.
precedents.topic: barrier removal priorities; counter and dining alternatives

precedents.case_name: ADA Guide for Small Businesses: Sales and Service Counters
precedents.citation: U.S. Dep't of Justice, ADA Guide for Small Businesses
precedents.holding: A counter section at least 36 in long and no more than 36 in high with a 30x48 in clear floor space makes a sales counter accessible; an auxiliary counter, folding shelf, or temporarily a clipboard can serve where lowering is not readily achievable.

verification.note: Publication year not shown on the excerpt page; 1999 is from memory.

precedents.case_name: Settlement Agreement between the United States and Jo-Ann Stores, Inc.
precedents.holding: The retailer agreed to a nationwide policy keeping movable displays and merchandise out of entrances, aisles and routes, and to survey and correct aisle widths and counter heights in its stores.
precedents.topic: maintenance of clear aisles in retail

statutes.summary: Statutory damages in construction-related accessibility claims are recoverable only for occasions the plaintiff personally encountered the violation or was deterred; assessed per occasion, not per violation; reducible to $1,000 (CASp-inspected, corrected within 60 days) or $2,000 (small business with 25 or fewer employees and under $3.5M receipts, corrected within 30 days).
Unruh Act damages: actual damages up to three times actual damages, but no less than $4,000 per offense, plus attorney's fees.
A violation of the right of any individual under the ADA also constitutes a violation of the Unruh Civil Rights Act.
Public accommodations must maintain accessible features in operable working condition; isolated or temporary interruptions for maintenance or repairs are not prohibited.
